paragraphs.text: Yesterday, lovers of Christ, we sang the praises of the coming of the holy and adorable Spirit. That coming is not honored by human notions; it is attested by the Father's power. For the word of God is not established by what we reason or utter, but by what enlightens us, and by this piety is established and the truth proclaimed. The word of God alone, the teaching of the Holy Spirit alone, is the lamp of piety, the proclamation of the knowledge of God, and the illumination of divine teaching. So we must dwell further on the explanation of the holy and adorable Spirit, and say something clearer about that holy and glorious Power. To use the same words again: the Holy Spirit is indivisible in nature, since he proceeded from the indivisible and undivided nature. This is what the divine words teach, or rather what the Spirit proclaims about himself, speaking through the prophets and shedding his own ray through the apostles.

His name is Holy Spirit, Spirit of truth, Spirit of God, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Father, Spirit of the Son, Spirit of Christ. This is what Scripture calls him, or rather what he calls himself: both Spirit of God and the Spirit who is from God. When we hear "Spirit of God," we might think he is called this only because he belongs to God. To prevent that, Scripture brings in the Holy Spirit and adds "from God" to "of God." "Of God" is one thing and "from God" another. Heaven and earth are "of God," since he made them. But nothing is said to be "from God" unless it is from his essence. So he is called Holy Spirit. This is his proper and primary title, the one with the most expressive meaning, which shows the nature of the Holy Spirit. Holy Spirit, Spirit of God. Who calls him Spirit of God? Listen to the Savior: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." Spirit of God. As I said before, someone hearing "Spirit of God" might think it means mere belonging and not a sharing of nature. To prevent that, Paul says: "But you have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God." Again, he is called Spirit of the Father, as the Savior tells the apostles: "Do not worry about how or what you will say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of our Father who speaks in you." Scripture said "Spirit of God" and then added "from God." In the same way, he is again called Spirit of the Father. And in case you think this is said only because he belongs to the Father, the Savior confirms it: "But when the Advocate comes, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father." There it was "from God," here it is "from the Father." He said of himself, "I came forth from the Father," and he said of the Holy Spirit, "who proceeds from the Father." So he is the Spirit of God and the Spirit of God the Father, and he proceeds from the Father. What does "proceeds" mean? He did not say "is begotten," and we must not think what is not written. The Son is begotten of the Father; the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

No doubt you want me to explain the difference: How was the one begotten? How did the other proceed? Well then: because you have learned that he was begotten, have you also learned how? Because you hear the Son proclaimed, have you grasped how he was begotten? These are names honored by faith and guarded by pious reasoning. So what is the force of "proceeds"? Scripture wants to avoid the word "begetting," so that it does not call him a son. So it says "Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father." It presents him as proceeding, like water gushing from the earth, as was said of paradise: "A river proceeds out of Eden." He proceeds and wells up. The Father is called a fountain of living water, as the prophet Jeremiah says: "Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered greatly, for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." By defining him as the fountain of living water, the divine word presented the Father as the fountain of life, from which the living water proceeds. "Who proceeds from the Father." What proceeds? The Holy Spirit. How? As water from a fountain. How do we know that the Holy Spirit is called water? The Savior says: "Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." And the evangelist explains this water, adding: "He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." The evangelist John, then, made it plain that the living water is the Holy Spirit. And the Father says, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water." So the Father is the fountain of the Spirit. That is why the Spirit proceeds from the Father. So he is called (I repeat it) Spirit of God and Spirit from God, Spirit of the Father and Spirit from the Father. Isaiah bears witness to the name "Spirit of the Lord," speaking in the person of Christ: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." And Paul says: "Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." If there is freedom wherever the Spirit comes, is he himself a slave? The Holy Spirit breaks the yoke of slavery for those he visits and grants them the standing of free people. How then can he be a slave? How can he give what he does not have? How can he set others free if he is a slave? Have you not heard Paul say: "For the law of the Spirit of life has set me free in Christ Jesus"? Does the Spirit set slaves free while not being free by nature himself? If he were created and enslaved, he could not set anyone free.

Do not let heretics outwit you. I do not call him a slave or a creature; that is a new heresy. They are in danger of introducing three first principles: one uncreated, one created, and a third I do not know what to call. Spirit of God, Spirit from God, Spirit of the Father, Spirit who proceeds from the Father, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Son. The apostle says: "And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, 'Abba, Father.'" There is the Spirit of the Son. Elsewhere Paul again speaks of the Spirit of Christ: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of Christ dwells in you." Please notice this holy interweaving. Paul has laid out a kind of holy and living chain of threefold power. He binds together the indivisible nature and shows one power under different names: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." There is "Spirit." "If indeed the Spirit of Christ dwells in you." There is "Spirit of God" [?]. "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ." Surely he ought to have said, "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of God." Yet he said "Spirit of Christ." He said "Spirit of God" and then added "the Spirit of Christ." "But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." He said this to show that where the Spirit is, Christ is too. For Christ to be present is the same as for the Spirit to be present, and to say "Spirit of God" is the same as to say "Spirit of Christ." So he is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, which is as much as to say the Spirit of the Son, since the Savior says: "I am the truth." He is called the Spirit of truth, which means the Spirit of the Son, as Paul says: "God has sent the Spirit of his Son." So he is both the Spirit of the Son and the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ. Listen to Paul himself: "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ dwells in you." These are the names of that holy and spotless Power, the holy and adorable Spirit. But there are other names too, which belong not to his nature but to his activity. The subject is deep and needs attentive, careful and faithful listening. The Spirit is also called Spirit of life, since the Savior says: "I am the truth and the life." He is called Spirit of life, as Paul also says: "For the law of the Spirit of life." These names belong to his very sovereignty, his very nature. But there are other names that are given not to the Holy Spirit himself but to his power and activity, such as his gifts. I will state the idea, make it clearer, and bring in the evidence. Suppose the Holy Spirit, through the prayers of the saints, grants sanctification to me or to another Christian. I receive a gift, so that my body and soul are holy. The gift given to me is called a spirit of holiness, that is, a grace-gift. Suppose the Holy Spirit gives someone a gift without wisdom or knowledge, giving him faith alone. There are many like this, with the gift of believing the Scriptures: they do not know the Scriptures, yet they believe them. That gift is called a spirit of faith. If someone receives from the Holy Spirit the power and gift to believe the promise of the good things that will be given in the age to come, he has received a spirit of promise. If someone receives the gift of wisdom, the gift is called a spirit of wisdom. Everywhere the gifts of the Spirit are called "spirit." Pay close attention, for we are explaining these insights only in part and in outline. Now let us come to the proofs. When someone has the gift of love, he is said to have a spirit of love. When someone receives the gift of martyrdom, he is said to have a spirit of power, that is, a grace-gift. Since the giver is the Holy Spirit, the gift, the grace, is called by the same name. That is why Paul says: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption." And again: "For he did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but a spirit of power and love and self-discipline." Here he uses "spirit" to mean the gift, as when he says: "You were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise." Where is "spirit of promise" written? Paul says: "Having the same spirit of faith and of promise," that is, the gift of the Spirit. So there you have a spirit of faith and a spirit of promise. If someone is gentle and humble of heart, he has received a gift of gentleness, and it is a grace-gift of God. Paul says this too: "If a person is caught in some transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness," that is, in the grace of the gift of gentleness. "Look to yourself," he says, "so that you too are not tempted." There is a spirit of gentleness. To another is given sanctification of soul and body, and this is called a spirit of holiness, as he says: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets, according to the spirit of holiness." He has put it in inverted order. The sense is this: Paul, who became an apostle according to the spirit of holiness. Many followed the first wording and took it to mean "who was designated Son of God according to the spirit of holiness." But that is not the meaning. Rather, it means: Paul, appointed an apostle according to the spirit of holiness. And when was he appointed? "From the resurrection of Jesus Christ." The other apostles were appointed before the Passion; he was appointed after the resurrection. Hence "according to the spirit of holiness." I will add something else. When we all begin to say, at the hour of the mysteries, "Our Father, who art in heaven," we have received a gift, the spirit of adoption, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. It is also called a spirit of zeal, as Paul says: "Since you too are zealous for spirits," that is, you are eager for spiritual gifts. "Since you are zealous for spirits," that is, for the gifts. "And I will show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am nothing." That is, love is greater than every gift.

But let us return to our subject. Here Isaiah comes in again, for the same Spirit speaks through them all. Paul spoke of a spirit of life, a spirit of love, a spirit of power, a spirit of self-discipline, a spirit of promise, a spirit of faith, a spirit of gentleness, a spirit of adoption. In the same way blessed Isaiah says: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse," meaning the Savior's royal rod. He calls the royal emblem a rod, as David says: "A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him."

Here is the name of the Spirit's own nature. Then come the gifts: "a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and might, a spirit of knowledge, a spirit of piety, a spirit of the fear of God." Take an example. You, a believer, or some other Christian, open a passage of Scripture with a hidden and obscure meaning. The Holy Spirit grants that the hidden meanings be revealed. That is a gift that reveals the depths. This is why the apostle, wanting the disciples of piety to understand the Scriptures, says: "I pray to God that he may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in knowledge, the eyes of your mind being enlightened." Do you see the spirit of revelation? But let us return to our subject. Where one must learn the depths, it is called a spirit of revelation. Where one must have love, it is called a spirit of love. Where the teacher must speak clearly, it is called a spirit of wisdom. Where the hearer must understand intelligently, it is called a spirit of understanding. The spirit of wisdom is given to those who teach, the spirit of understanding to those who listen. I preach; you know how to understand but not how to teach. The gift of wisdom is so called because it teaches. God sends the teacher a word of wisdom, and in the same way he sends the learner a gift of understanding, so that the learner may understand the things of God. To show this, he says: "The preaching mouth has the grace of wisdom; the learning heart has the grace of understanding." Wisdom is the weapon of the mouth; understanding is the weapon of the heart. That is why David says: "My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding." Another person did not receive the grace of teaching, but received the grace to give good and admirable advice and counsel. Sometimes the teacher does not know how to give advice, because he did not receive that gift. No one receives everything, so that no one may think grace is a matter of nature. One receives the grace of teaching, and so that he is not puffed up, he finds himself weak when it comes to counsel in practical affairs. Another cannot teach, but gives good counsel. So the one who lends to others finds himself borrowing elsewhere. Where can we see this? I will now show you that one who has received the grace of teaching needs someone else's advice. Moses received a spirit of wisdom, of lawgiving, of teaching, and he took it upon himself to judge the people all day long. Then Jethro his father-in-law comes and advises him: "You cannot judge so great a people alone. You will wear yourself out completely if you do this. What should you do? Appoint leaders of tens and of fifties and of hundreds and of thousands. Then the leader of ten can refer to the leader of fifty whatever is beyond him. The leader of fifty can refer to the leader of a thousand whatever is beyond him. The leader of a thousand can refer to you whatever is beyond him. And whatever is beyond you, you will refer to God." "If there is any difficult matter," he says, "they will bring it to you; and if anything is too hard for you, you will bring it to God." And the lawgiver, wise as he was, accepted a layman's advice. That advice became law and an image of things to come. Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had been a priest of idols. Later he rejected that error, learned the truth, and became an image of the Church of the Gentiles. He shows that the understanding of the Gentiles surpasses the wisdom of the Law, not because they are Gentiles but because they have repented. For when was Jethro's advice accepted? Not while he was a priest, but after he had come to know God. When he saw God's works and Moses told him of the wonders in Egypt, he said: "Now I know" (see his repentance) "that the Lord your God is great above all gods." So from the moment he knew the truth, he received the gift of good counsel.

But let us return to our subject. The one who teaches received the spirit of wisdom, and the one who is taught received the spirit of understanding, so that he may understand. That is why Isaiah assigns wisdom to the one who speaks and understanding to the one who hears, saying: "A wise master builder and an understanding hearer." The spirit of counsel is given to the one who gives advice, and the spirit of strength to the one who receives the advice. The adviser receives grace to say something good. The one who receives the advice receives grace to carry out what is beneficial. The spirit of the fear of God. Each of these gifts was given to meet the need at hand. Take the building of the tabernacle under Moses in the wilderness: there was no need there for a gift of teaching, but for a gift of craftsmanship, so that they would know how to weave the fine linen, the blue, the scarlet and the purple. God gave the grace of the gifts of master building, weaving, loom-work, goldsmithing, stone-cutting and embroidery. And why did he give these crafts? Because God was making the tabernacle on earth. The tabernacle was an image of heaven and earth, and in six days God made heaven and earth. The tabernacle was being built as a figure of heaven and earth, and what was needed was a gift of the Holy Spirit suited to the task. It was not the time for teaching, but for weaving and the other crafts. And God says: "See, I have called by name Bezalel of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with a divine spirit, a spirit of wisdom and knowledge and perception." Wisdom, so that he could instruct the workers to work in such and such a way or to make this or that. Knowledge, so that he could fit things together. Perception, so that he could grasp the force of what God was saying. Elsewhere God promises to give the grace of loving-kindness, saying: "I will pour out on the house of David a spirit of grace and compassion," that is, a gift of loving-kindness. Again, he bestows a gift of humility. Where do we see this? In the three young men in the furnace. As righteous men they trod down the flame, yet as humble men they called themselves sinners. Their surpassing righteousness let them tread down the flame and turn the furnace into dew, yet they were not puffed up. They did not say: "Oh, how righteousness is on our side! We have conquered nature; we have gone beyond the law." Instead they act as righteous men and speak as sinners. Just think: they trod down the flame and danced like saints, and confessed like sinners: "We have sinned, we have done lawlessly, we have done wrong. All that you have brought upon us you have done in true judgment, for we have done lawlessly in turning away from you, and we have not listened to your commandments, so that it might go well with us." So because they humbled themselves even though they were righteous, they received a spirit of humility, a gift of humility. That is why, when they saw the grace, they say that "at this time we have no prophet, no offering, no incense, no place to make an offering and find mercy." Since we have no city, no temple, no altar, no incense, humility will suffice us in place of them all. That is why they say: "But with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be accepted." Of another, who is full of grace and has received the gift in its entirety, Scripture says: "He received a spirit of fullness." Where do we find this? Jeremiah says: "The way of the daughter of my people leads not to holiness, nor to purity, a spirit of fullness." They do not have, he means, the spirit that fills them. In the same way the apostles had a spirit of fullness, as it is written: "Then Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit," when he rebukes Elymas the sorcerer. Do you see the gifts? So I repeat the names of the ineffable nature: Spirit of God, the Spirit who is from God, Spirit of the Lord, Spirit of the Father, Spirit of the Son, Spirit of Christ, Spirit of the one who raised Christ, Spirit of life, Spirit of truth. Then the gifts: spirit of power, spirit of love, spirit of self-control, spirit of promise, spirit of faith, spirit of revelation, spirit of adoption. When someone receives the gift of judging, he has received a spirit of judgment, as Isaiah says: "And the Lord will cleanse them with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." He calls the power that punishes and cleanses a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. David asks for a right spirit, the spirit that leads to uprightness. He also asks for a gift that rules over the passions and keeps the soul from being enslaved to them. David's heart had been turned aside: he had fallen from self-control into the evil of passion and pleasure, he had unjustly decided that the man should be killed, he had become a slave of desire and turned to adultery. So he asks for a right spirit, saying: "Renew it within my inmost being, and do not cast me away from your presence; restore to me the joy of your salvation, and establish me with a governing spirit," that is, with a gift that governs the passions and masters the pleasures.

This is what we have said about the divine authority of the Holy Spirit and the differences among his workings. But the heretics do not realize that when Scripture speaks of a "spirit of holiness" or "of promise" it is referring to the gifts. Instead they apply these to the nature, saying that God gave and bestowed the Holy Spirit. "Do you see," they say, "that he is a gift of God?" They read what concerns the gifts and applied it to the nature, when they ought to have understood which names indicate the nature and which names express the grace. They have peddled the truth, thrown everything into confusion, overturned themselves, and run aground away from the truth. "Their senseless heart was darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools." So they go on: "Since you raise the question of the Spirit and teach from the Scriptures, and want to have the Scriptures as your witnesses, we too, on the basis of the Scriptures themselves, cite what the Savior said about the Holy Spirit." What then does he say? "When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will declare to you; for he will take from what is mine and declare it to you." "Do you see," the heretic says, "how he does not speak on his own, but takes from him? Can the authority of the Spirit possibly be demonstrated? Has not Scripture shown that he is subject to the authority of the Son, that he borrows from him and supplies it to others?" Pay close attention. When something said seems puzzling to you, do not pounce on the wording at once, but wait for the thought to be completed. Have you not seen how, while a building is being prepared, everything lies jumbled together: lime, stones, timber? To your eye everything is jumbled, but to the builder everything is in order. He knows the moment when he will fit this jumbled piece to that one, and that one to this. And the scattered pieces, once they take their proper arrangement, produce the beauty of the building. So when you see the speaker passing from this point to that, and from that to another, realize that he is preparing his materials. Once I have laid out the materials, then I show how they fit together. There is one nature of the Son and the Spirit, one power, one truth, one life, one wisdom. But from the time the Savior deigned to take our created nature, he is filled with the Holy Spirit. This is not because he is inferior to the Holy Spirit, but because the flesh had to receive the coming of the Spirit in human fashion. It is not that God the Word could not sanctify the created nature he had assumed. If you follow that line of reasoning, the Son too is superfluous, for the Father would have been enough to sanctify the creature. Surely the Father does not take the Son as a helper because he is weak? Surely the Son does not take the Spirit as a helper because he is weak? No: since there is one nature working all things in all, some things the Father does, and they are understood to belong to the whole nature; some the Son does, and they extend to the whole nature; some the Spirit does, and they are attributed to the whole nature. When the nature is considered in itself, it is equal and uniform, full of sovereign authority, wondrous, neither lacking nor imperfect, neither advancing nor diminishing nor lessening, receiving no additions. But when God the Word assumes the flesh that comes from us, he makes it receive the Holy Spirit in human fashion, like one of the prophets or one of the apostles. I said this beforehand: it is not that the Son's divinity was insufficient, but that the knowledge of the Trinity might be shown complete in this created nature. So the Lord's flesh was deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit, and the Savior then wished to make the nature he had assumed the Holy Spirit's own, so that whatever Christ did according to the flesh might be ascribed to the Holy Spirit who dwelt in him as in a holy human temple. For he is man for our sake, but God in his own right; God in his own right, but man out of love for humanity. He cast out demons and wished to ascribe their expulsion to the Holy Spirit, saying: "But if I cast out demons by the Holy Spirit." He did not say "by God the Word," but ascribes it to the Holy Spirit, as a holy man deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit. So too, when he entered the temple, he takes the prophet Isaiah and reads, and what he reads is what was written about himself. "And unrolling the book," it says, he reads: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." Does this really befit God the Word? Does God say, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me"? Is it not beyond dispute that it is the person of the man who is speaking? "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." I was anointed, he says, by the Holy Spirit. That is why Peter says: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power."

Let us keep our minds on this, I beg you. All of this is preparation for "he will take from what is mine." We have not wandered from one subject to another; as I said before, I am getting the materials ready so that you can fit them together. He was deemed worthy of the Holy Spirit. He was baptized in the Jordan, and John says: "I saw the heavens opened and the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining on him." Do you see how he receives the Holy Spirit in human fashion? No one is so impious as to think that the divinity received the Spirit. John the Baptist says: "Among you stands one whom you do not know, and I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me: 'The one on whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining on him, this is my Son.'" The Holy Spirit came down so that Isaiah's words might be fulfilled: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." The flesh was baptized, and as soon as he was baptized he came up from the water and was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness. He was led up, and the flesh had the Holy Spirit as its guide. Why was he led? To give you a pattern: "Just as my flesh is not led by desires but led by the Spirit, so you too ought to be." That is why Paul too says: "But if you are led by the Spirit of God, you are no longer in the flesh," and "Those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law." The flesh of Christ is led; let us be led as well. This is why he takes everything upon himself: to leave us a pattern. He was led up by the Spirit to be tempted, and he conquered the devil. It was not the divinity that conquered, for it would be an insult to the divinity to say, "I have conquered." God is never defeated, nor does he win victories; he always rules. If he can win a victory, then he could certainly also be defeated. But the one who always rules is the Almighty: those he rules do not rise up against him, and he does not have to labor to prevail over his subjects. So if the Lord's flesh, the Lord's created nature, the strange man, the heavenly one, the new shoot that blossomed from a strange birth, receives the Holy Spirit, you have the testimony that the Spirit came from heaven and led him up to overcome the devil. So that the image of Adam, which had been led astray in the beginning, might now conquer, the strange man entered the contest escorted by the power of the Spirit. That is why, just as Scripture said, "He was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted," so, when he returned as victor, it says: "And Jesus returned from the wilderness in the power of the Spirit." So the flesh had the Holy Spirit, not a share of the gifts as we do, wisdom to one and knowledge to another, but it had all the gifts. In truth I am anxious and tremble that the weakness of my tongue may blunt the greatness of what is being proclaimed. The Lord's body, then, the holy flesh, when it received the working of the Holy Spirit, did not receive one grace or [?] a second, as the apostles and prophets did. For a human being cannot contain everything. That is why Paul says: "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Do all have gifts of healing?" Among us the gifts are divided. But in the flesh of Christ were all the graces, all the gifts, in keeping with the substance of the flesh. And pay attention: first he filled his own temple with every grace. He had the gift of healing diseases, casting out demons, raising the dead, prophesying, doing the works of truth. He could do everything and had the fullness of the gifts, from the time the Lord's flesh was filled with all the gifts. And it was altogether necessary that we receive in part, as from a reservoir, from the Lord's body; from it gifts are supplied to apostles and prophets alike. John testified that in him is the whole fullness of the divinity, and Paul says: "In whom the whole fullness of the divinity dwelt bodily." He did not simply say, "in whom the divinity dwelt," but "the fullness of the divinity," that is, every gift of the divinity.

And so that no one might think it dwelt in God the Word, he says: "In whom the whole fullness of the divinity dwelt bodily." In his flesh was the whole fullness of wisdom, understanding, power, signs, every kind of working. And so we all borrow from that fullness. John the Baptist testifies: "And I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize said to me: 'The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining' (he did not say 'granting him one gift,' but 'remaining' in full), 'this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire.'" Then John, wishing to show that the Savior did not receive grace as a mere man does, says: "God does not give the Spirit by measure; the Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hand." Where, then, do we receive from? "From his fullness we have all received." He is the fullness; we receive from the fullness. How? From the time he filled the Lord's flesh, he drew from it as from a spring and lent the gift to human beings. Pay attention, I beg you. So he says: "When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will take from what is mine."

Pay attention to the precision of the wording. He did not say, “from me,” but “from what is mine.” “From me”: from whom? [?] “From what is mine he will give you”? No: “he will take.” He takes, but not as one who borrows. Since he filled the spring as the source of the gifts, he draws from the reservoir and supplies everyone from what is his own. And how do we know that this taking is a taking from what is one’s own? Listen. God filled Moses with the Spirit, and Moses says, “I cannot carry the burden of this people alone; appoint someone else for yourself.” God says to him, “Choose seventy elders, and I will take some of the Spirit that is in you and put it upon them.” He did not say, “I will take what is yours,” but “some of the Spirit that is in you”: I will take from what is mine. God says, “In those days I will pour out some of my Spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy.” If God borrowed when he took from Moses, then the Spirit borrowed when it took from the Son. For Moses was a type of Christ: just as the seventy came from Moses, so the whole world received the Holy Spirit from Christ. “He will take from what is mine”: from what it supplied to me alone, to the Lord’s own humanity, the very one who gave it will take. It came and remained on me, anointed me, sanctified me, led me into the desert, and brought me back a victor. “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you.” And to show that he was not speaking of the Holy Spirit but of the gifts, right after saying, “He will take from what is mine,” he immediately adds, “All that the Father has is mine.” I received these things from the Holy Spirit. That is why I said, “He will take from what is mine.” God sanctified the flesh by the Holy Spirit, and the Father sent the gift of the Spirit into the flesh of Christ. When the grace came, it placed all the gifts in Christ. That is why he says, “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you.” What, then, does “He will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will make known to you” mean? It was said earlier that the Holy Spirit is one thing and the gift another, just as the king is one thing and the king’s gift another. When someone is at war with many different barbarian nations, he is at a loss where to begin. If he turns his attention to these, another flank rises against him. If he divides himself into two parts, his forces are split. We stand between the Arians, who reject the glory of Christ, and the Macedonians, who insult the divine glory of the Spirit. If I treat what concerns the Son as agreed, as I would with the Macedonians, the Arian at once attacks: “Have you convinced me about the Son, that you are talking to me about the Spirit?”

But our subject today is the Holy Spirit. By the grace given by Christ we have often won the argument about the Son, and you are witnesses of what was said: it was not clever sophistry but proof from the Scriptures. I would have liked to build up the argument about the Son now as well, for its power always shines out of itself. But for the sake of convincing the heretics who limp where the Spirit is concerned, I pass over it for the present. Yet it is impossible for someone who limps about the Spirit to walk straight about the Son. To this day you cannot persuade a single Macedonian to sign the “one in being” of Nicaea, even though they always say, “We keep to that faith,” because nothing was spelled out there about the Spirit. At that time there was no contest or war over it. Still, to convince them, I say this. It is written, “He will not speak on his own.” Say to the Macedonian: this is written about the Son too. Better, he says it about himself: “I do not speak on my own.” Pay attention, I beg you. I am drawing the testimony from what you yourself admit. Against the Arian, a contest is needed over “I do not speak on my own,” and over the Spirit too. But with you, who profess to be orthodox, no contest is needed. When you argue about Christ you call him equal to God, like the Father in all things. So I have put the question to you as to someone who confesses his glory. You say about the Spirit, “He will not speak on his own.” The Savior says about himself, “I do not speak on my own, but whatever I have heard from my Father, that is what I speak.” See, the Son too does not speak on his own. So far, equal honor. I say this to you. The Arian is at a loss over both. What happens to people who are shipwrecked happens to unbelievers, as Paul says: “who have made shipwreck of their faith.” The Arians, shipwrecked, have lost both the glory of Christ and the power of the Holy Spirit. The Macedonians are struggling to climb out, but they have lost half the cargo, as Paul says: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” Pay attention, then, so that we do not seem to be attacking for the sake of the fight, or to be making our proof with insults. “I do not speak on my own.” Explain to me what “I do not speak on my own” means. In what sense did the Savior say it? Whatever explanation the Macedonian comes up with for the Son, let him apply the same to the Holy Spirit. The two stand evenly balanced: neither does the Spirit speak on its own, nor the Son on his own. But the Son has need of the Father, and the Spirit too has need of the Father. So far, equal honor. Pay attention, then. I know I have launched myself into deep water, as the power of Christ, which searches all things, has seen. I tremble more than I speak, for fear that the vessel may run out into a boundless abyss and there may be no wind of the Spirit. Suppose the ship is ready: the helmsman, the sailors, the ropes, the anchors, everything prepared, and nowhere a breath of wind. Does not all that equipment lie idle when the working of the wind is absent? So it is here. There may be breadth of speech, depth of thought, fine expression and insight, but if the Holy Spirit is not present to supply them, everything lies idle.

Why, then, did he say about himself, as he also said about the Spirit, “I do not speak on my own”? We have put our opponent to shame in debate. Now let us convince both ourselves and them, if indeed they will be convinced. We would certainly not force them, but let us speak, in case they may be persuaded. And do not be surprised that I, a mere man, say this. God says to Ezekiel, “Go to the house of Israel and speak to them, in case they may listen, in case they may believe.” We say these things in case they may listen, in case they may believe, in case they may agree. And if they do not agree after these things have been said, we are innocent. This is how Paul taught, and after teaching he says, “I testify to you all that I am clean of the blood of all of you, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the way of God.” And now I ask: why did the Savior say, “I do not speak on my own,” and about the Spirit, “He will not speak on his own”? I beg you, my beloved, let us fix our minds on this. Although there is one Christ, many false christs came forward, as the Savior said: “Many will come in my name, false christs and false prophets.” So although there is one Christ, whose coming was promised through the prophets, some deceivers appeared before his coming, saying, “We are he.” Theudas says, “I am he”; Judas the Galilean says, “I am he”; and they led many astray. When the Savior came, he says, “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.” Those earlier men were deceivers. They put on the name of Christ and worked hard to persuade the people that they were the Christ. They did not appear together but each on his own, one appearing at one time and another at another. So Christ says, “All who came before me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them. My sheep hear my voice; they know my voice and follow me.” Those false christs came and did not teach from the law or from the prophets. They spoke from themselves and from their own opinion. When the Savior came, he did not depart from the law or from the prophets. He said, for example, “Isaiah spoke well,” and again, “Is it not written in your law?” And when the devil approached him, he says to him, “It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.” So when Christ came in the flesh, he did not speak on his own, but from the prophets. Those who came before Christ in the name of Christ did not speak from the law or from the prophets; they spoke the things of error from their own opinion. So the Savior says, “I do not speak on my own,” as they did. To speak on one’s own is to speak outside the law. That is how we too must speak. When you see heretics bringing up Aristotelian or Platonic arguments, say, “We do not speak on our own. What we have heard from Christ is what we declare.” And how do we know that one who speaks on his own is a false prophet, or that speaking on one’s own is the mark of a false prophet? The prophet Ezekiel says, “As I live, says the Lord, I am against the prophets who lead my people astray. I did not send them; they spoke on their own, and they utter what comes from their own heart.” Since the false prophets preached on their own, the Savior throws off that suspicion and says, “I do not speak on my own.” How do we know that the Savior was suspected of being a deceiver? Let us establish this first. At the feast of Tabernacles the crowds were looking for Jesus and saying, “Where is he?” And there was disagreement about him. Some said, “He is a good man”; others said, “No, he is leading the crowd astray.” Do you see how he was suspected of being a deceiver? Again, after the death of the holy Savior, the chief priests say to Pilate, “Sir, we know that that deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’” I have said this to show that he was thought to be a deceiver. Since he was thought a deceiver, he says, “I do not speak on my own,” but from the law and from the prophets: “whatever I have heard from the Father.” He does not mean that he heard it from the Father according to his Godhead; he heard it in the law and in the prophets. He speaks in the person of the flesh, to dispel the error. “I do not speak on my own, but whatever I have heard from the Father. But you speak what you have heard from your father the devil.” And to show that when the devil speaks he produces falsehood in some people, he says, “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own.” “I do not speak on my own,” but from the prophets and from the law. For this is truth. So just as the Savior, to dispel the suspicion and throw off that evil charge, says, “I do not speak on my own,” as the deceivers did, so too he speaks about the Spirit.

Now let us fix our minds here, I beg you. In the case of the Savior, many false christs and false prophets appear. One man said, “I am he,” and another, “I am he,” as it is written: “Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray; but do not be led astray.” Just as the name of Christ came to be claimed by deceivers, so many were going to pretend to have the Holy Spirit when they did not, and to speak. But in the first case a man appeared and said, “I am the Christ.” Here, no one dared to say, “I am the Holy Spirit.” For the Spirit did not come in a body; it came to dwell invisibly. It came upon Peter, it came upon Paul, and it was acknowledged that they had the Spirit of the Lord. Then Simon popped up and said, “I have the Spirit.” By looking, no one could tell who had no spirit, who had an unclean spirit, or who had the Holy Spirit. If the Spirit had a visible form, he could not have slipped in by stealth, for he would have been exposed by examination. Montanus came, saying, “I have the Holy Spirit.” The Manichaean came, saying, “I have the Holy Spirit.” But it was not obvious. So that people would not be led astray by the name, since the gift was going to come invisibly, he says, “When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will remind you of my words and guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own.” If you see someone who says, “I have the Holy Spirit,” but does not speak the things of the Gospel, only his own, he is speaking on his own, and the Holy Spirit is not in him. Just as he says about himself, “I do not speak on my own,” to dispel the suspicion of deception, so, to separate error from truth and to show who has the Holy Spirit and who does not but only pretends to have it, he says, “He will not speak on his own.” You have heard from me what I handed down. When the invisible Spirit comes, it will speak what is mine. If you see someone repeating the things of the Gospel, he truly has the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit comes to remind you of what I taught. So if any of those who claim to have the Spirit says something on his own, and not from the Gospels, do not believe him. Keep to my teaching: “He will not speak on his own.” Rather, the coming of the Spirit that takes place shows who has received the Holy Spirit and who has not. If someone repeats the things of Christ, he has the Holy Spirit. For no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit. Mani came, truly a maniac, whose name aptly fits his error, and he says, “I am the Paraclete whom the Savior promised to the apostles; I am the Son of God.” Where did you hear in the Gospel of Jesus Christ that the sun and the moon are creators? Where did Christ say that they draw up souls and carry them on high? Where have you read that? From the fact that he does not say what is written but speaks on his own, it is clear that he does not have the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit “will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will declare to you”; that is, he will confirm what I have spoken. And see how wonderful this is. Just as the Savior, when he came, became the fulfillment of the law and the prophets, so the Spirit is the fulfillment of the Gospel. When Christ came, he confirmed what came from the Father, what was said in the law and the prophets. That is why Paul says, “Christ is the fulfillment of the law.” When the Holy Spirit came, it fulfilled the things of the Gospel. Whatever is in the law, Christ fulfills; whatever is in Christ’s teaching, the Spirit fulfills. This is not because the Father was incomplete. Rather, just as Christ appeared to confirm the things of the Father, so the Holy Spirit appeared to confirm the things of the Son. How do we know this? The Savior says to the disciples, “I have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Holy Spirit comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own.” For he fulfills what is mine. The Son fills up what belongs to the Father and does not speak on his own; the Spirit fills up what belongs to the Son and does not speak on his own. And if you hear him saying, “I will send you the Holy Spirit,” do not take it as referring to the Godhead. For God is not sent. These are names that signify activity, names that are both hidden and shining: hidden in their dignity, shining in contemplation. For example, everyone who sends someone sends him to places where he himself is not present. Suppose that I, who am speaking, am in this seat. I cannot say to someone, “Come, I will send you here.” That is not sending; it is seating him beside me or standing him next to me. But if God is everywhere (for he says, “I fill heaven and earth”), where does the one who is everywhere send? “If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present; if I take my wings at dawn and settle at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will guide me.” Where, then, does God send? Or is it that he himself is everywhere, but the one sent is not everywhere? “God sent his Son into the world.” As though he were not present in the world? Yet the world comes from the Son. Did he come into the world, then, as though he had not been in the world before? How then does John the evangelist say, “All things came into being through him. He was in the world, and the world came into being through him”? How then was he sent into the world? Again, if the one sent was sent, and the sender stayed above while the one sent was below, how could he say, “And the one who sent me is with me”?

Pay attention carefully, I beg you. Make the argument secure. For the heretic can say, “He is with me by his help,” just as I too say, “God is with me.” But he did not say it simply. What did he say? “The Father who abides in me.” If he was with him and abode in him, how did the one send, or how was the other sent? Either they came, in which case both came and no one was sent; or else both stayed. If the Father stayed above, how does the Son say, “The Father is with me”? If the sender stayed above, how does the one sent have the sender with him? For he said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is with me.” How, then, was he sent who says, “The Father is in me”? And again, how did the Father send? So when he says, “I will send you the Holy Spirit,” he means the gift of the Spirit. And so that you may learn that it is the gift that is sent, while the Spirit is not sent, the Savior says to the apostles, “Stay in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high, and you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” The power that is supplied is one thing; the Spirit who supplies it is another. “For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually just as it wills.” You cannot show the Holy Spirit being sent in its bare Godhead. But if I show you the maker of heaven and earth being sent by the Holy Spirit, what will you do? Either deny Christ and erase the Scriptures, or, as a servant of the Scriptures, submit to the Scriptures. “And where,” he says, “is this said?” Listen to God speaking through the prophet Isaiah, the herald of true religion: “Listen to me, Jacob, and Israel, whom I call: I am God, the first, and I am hereafter, and besides me there is no God.” Pay attention, for here at last is the point in question. Who, then, is the one who said this? The Father or the Son? See how, under the form of a single rule, he proclaims the Trinity in a veiled way: “I am God, the first, and I am hereafter, and besides me there is no God.” Who is saying this? The Creator. For he goes on: “With my hand I laid the foundation of the earth.” See how the Creator speaks: “And my Spirit established the heavens. I gave orders to all the stars; I raised up a king in righteousness, and all my ways are straight.” Having called himself the Creator and maker of heaven and earth, he then says this: “From the beginning I have not spoken these things to you in secret, nor in a dark place,” having said, I laid the foundation of the earth and made the heavens; “when they came into being, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” You, who made heaven and earth, who spoke to the stars, say, “The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” He begot you according to the Godhead; he sent you according to the flesh. The maker of heaven says, “The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” The heretic takes the sending of the Spirit as an insult. The Father sent without moving away, without moving the one sent; the Son sent the Spirit without dividing it and without being divided. That is why Scripture says, “God poured out his Spirit,” that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Godhead is not poured out; the gift is. That is why, to show that what is poured out is not the Holy Spirit but the grace of the divine Spirit, David says to Christ, “Grace is poured out on your lips.” Grace is poured out, not the one who gives the grace. So if equal honor is proclaimed, and “on his own” has been made clear, and “he will take from what is mine” has been explained as drawing from a reservoir, let the heretics have no room or way to slip in their impiety. Honor the Holy Spirit whom you have received. I have often said that you received something in exchange. Christ took from you your human nature, and he gave you his own Holy Spirit. Savile also has the complete text, vol. 6, p. 741f. He honored your nature by seating it at the right hand of the Father, and you have put his Spirit in the rank of a slave. This is what the saving law teaches. The prophets declare it, the apostles decree it, the martyrs confess it, the devout believe it, the Church assents to it; ingratitude fights against it, the faithful are fully convinced of it, and Christ is glorified. To him belong glory, honor and worship, together with the Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
